title: How Salesforce Untangled Its Own Data Chaos
summary: In episode 1032 of the SuperDataScience podcast, Jon Krohn discusses with Michael Andrew, CDO at Salesforce how Salesforce tackled its internal data chaos, including duplicate records and disparate systems, leading to the development and deployment of their Data 360 product. Michael explains how they unified customer data from various sources like Snowflake, Amazon data lake, and multiple Salesforce instances to create a single, actionable customer view. This integration now allows their sales team to receive proactive alerts, such as when a customer is about to run out of credits, demonstrating the power of a connected data strategy.

title: Cheaper Tokens Won't Shrink Your AI Bill
summary: In episode 1031 of the SuperDataScience podcast, Jon Krohn discusses with Ish Shah, Director at Dell how cheaper AI tokens won't necessarily reduce your overall AI expenditure. This clip highlights the increasing consumption of AI resources despite advancements in efficiency.

title: Convolutional Neural Networks for Computer Vision: Wolfram U Course Preview
summary: Check out this interactive course on convolutional neural networks for computer vision, taught using Wolfram Language and Notebook technology. Wolfram U instructor Arben Kalziqi gives a taste of what each section covers — from how images are represented internally to neural net encoders, decoders, layers, training and design — along with how Wolfram Language's built-in tools let you take a neural network apart layer by layer and visualize it with a graph-based system, all without leaving your Wolfram Notebook. You'll also see how to pull pretrained and untrained models straight from Wolfram’s Neural Net Repository and adapt them with transfer learning. This course is one of eight in the full Foundations of AI microcredential and includes the Wolfram AI Course Assistant to answer questions as you work through the lessons. Ready to start learning? title: How Many Iterations Does a Good Spec Need?
summary: A strong specification rarely emerges fully formed. It improves through focused iteration—clarifying assumptions, resolving ambiguity, testing edge cases, and aligning the intended outcome with real constraints. Hari Krishnan, author of Spec-Driven Development, explains how teams can refine a specification and why there’s no universal number of iterations. The goal isn’t perfection—it’s reaching the point where developers and AI coding agents have enough shared context to implement the right solution confidently. Learn more about Spec-Driven Development: https://hubs.la/Q04ypXVz0 #SpecDrivenDevelopment #AICoding #ContextEngineering #SoftwareDevelopment #CodingAgents #Shorts

title: SLMs, Fine-Tuning & LLMOps: Building Production-Ready Language Models
summary: Not every use case needs a large model. Smaller and purpose-built is often faster, cheaper and better suited to the job. Terms covered: - SLM (Small Language Model): fewer parameters, trading breadth for precision. Runs on-premises or on edge devices with no cloud dependency. - SLM Development: designing, training and optimizing a small model for a well-defined task or dataset - Fine-Tuning Engine: taking a pre-trained model and training it further on domain-specific data, so it learns the language of law, medicine or your business - LLMOps: the infrastructure and practices for deploying, managing, monitoring and updating language models over time A hospital running clinical documentation on local servers. A manufacturer processing quality reports on factory floor devices. These are where compact models win. — AI Fundamentals Glossary | H2O.ai University Full playlist: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLAWKlIKS-66E Free courses and certifications: https://h2o.ai/university #SLM #FineTuning #LLMOps #AIGlossary #H2Oai
summary_html:
Not every use case needs a large model. Smaller and purpose-built is often faster, cheaper and better suited to the job.

Terms covered:
- SLM (Small Language Model): fewer parameters, trading breadth for precision. Runs on-premises or on edge devices with no cloud dependency.
- SLM Development: designing, training and optimizing a small model for a well-defined task or dataset
- Fine-Tuning Engine: taking a pre-trained model and training it further on domain-specific data, so it learns the language of law, medicine or your business
- LLMOps: the infrastructure and practices for deploying, managing, monitoring and updating language models over time

A hospital running clinical documentation on local servers. A manufacturer processing quality reports on factory floor devices. These are where compact models win.

title: How a Voice Agent Learns the Rhythm of Conversation — Shawn Wen
summary: Tsung-Hsien (Shawn) Wen, CTO of PolyAI, tells Tim Scarfe why voice agents are harder than text agents. Voice adds time, and a good conversation depends on adapting to the person on the line, not just on reasoning to the best answer. Shawn describes an audio-native model (Dialog-RSN-1) that first predicts a turn-taking signal, then replies in text with citations, and writes the transcript last so enterprises can audit it. Along the way: training on real, noisy calls with synthetic noise added, and why over-cleaned audio made the new model worse. Latency, and what a voice agent should do while it thinks. Why a voice with a hint of regional accent beats a generic one. Why public benchmarks fall short for voice, why enterprises want to own their agent harness, and whether behaviour belongs in the harness or in the weights. The last stretch is about working with agents: cognitive debt, the shift from producing content to checking it, Wispr Flow, building tools that agents can use, and whether slop is in the eye of the reader. title: The Caveman Prompting Challenge
summary: Caveman prompting has one rule: why use many words when few do the trick? It saves tokens on the way in and on the way out. Push it too far, though, and the output falls apart. So how far is too far? Nobody has benchmarked it yet, and that question opens our conversation with James Barney, Head of Forward Labs at MetLife. James spends his days connecting new AI capabilities to old business problems across dozens of regulatory regimes, and he still finds time to push code. He explains how the FinOps Foundation's AI working group took on the most basic question: which model for which workload, and why the answer always comes down to cost, speed, and accuracy. We get into Anthropic's launch pricing for Fable, why a million tokens is easy to price and hard to explain, and why every stakeholder eventually tells you what they really care about once you name the wrong North Star. From there it gets practical. Start with the smartest model, then step down and add harness until quality holds. Treat exploration tokens like local builds and production tokens like pipelines. Govern agents the way you govern people, with proactive blocks, reactive checks, and policy as code an agent can actually read. We close on a bigger shift. When a chat window can pull from every dashboard at once, do we still need dashboards? James thinks mostly not, with one catch he calls the latent shopper problem: some insights only come from browsing data you did not know to ask about. title: Meet The Startup: Probabl: by the Creators of Scikit-Learn
summary: The creators of scikit-learn are GPU-accelerating machine learning — and partnering with NVIDIA to do it. Yann Lechelle, co-founder of Probabl, sat down with us to share why the team behind the world's most downloaded ML framework is doubling down on statistical machine learning — not generative AI — and what that means for the future of tabular data. Scikit-learn has surpassed 5 billion downloads, with 1.3 million GitHub projects depending on it. It's the backbone of data science as we know it. But it was built for CPUs — and the world has changed. Probabl is now offloading key algorithms to GPU, leveraging the Array API as an abstraction layer so that new generations of NVIDIA chips plug in seamlessly, without rewriting everything from scratch. Their new product, Skore, wraps scikit-learn and tabular large models into a unified ML platform — with the goal of becoming the world's leading tabular AI company within five years. And as Yann points out, it's not just data scientists using these tools anymore: agents are now the largest driver of scikit-learn downloads, consuming documentation and frameworks at machine speed. title: Gemini 4 Argon: The New Frontier

It's rolling out first to trusted testers through Google's Fairwind program. Fun fact: argon is the third most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere. summary_html:
Gemini 4 Argon can generate up to 1 million output tokens in a single response, up from 64K in earlier Gemini models. Most frontier models today cap a single response at around 128K.

Arena's testing puts Argon on the Pareto frontier of performance vs. cost: 33% lower cost per task than GPT-6.1 Sol and 70% lower than Claude Opus 5.5.

Argon isn't publicly available yet. It's rolling out first to trusted testers through Google's Fairwind program.

Fun fact: argon is the third most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere.
